archetype.name: Fringe Contender (shootout offense)
archetype.definition: A Detroit team whose passing offense can outscore almost anyone, but whose bottom-tier defense turns games against real opponents into coin flips in a division where everyone is winning.

report.headline: Elite Goff offense, leaky defense: a 5-2 record that flatters a coin-flip team
report.take:
This is the Lions' offense-first identity again. Jared Goff is running a top-three passing attack (0.264 EPA per dropback, 3rd), behind a line that allows pressure on just 17.5% of dropbacks (4th). Amon-Ra St. Brown is the clear first read at 76 targets, and Jahmyr Gibbs carries the ground game on 157 carries. The scoreboard follows: 30.7 points a game, 2nd in the league, and a passing game that has topped 300 yards several times. Special teams adds to it, ranked 2nd at 4.64 EPA a game, which quietly hands the offense better field position than it would otherwise have.

The other side is the problem. The defense ranks 31st in EPA allowed, 30th in explosive pass rate allowed, 28th on third down and 27th in red-zone touchdown rate. Its pieces don't fit together. The pass rush is real, with 21 sacks (2nd) and a 26.1% pressure rate (7th), and the tackling is the best in the league by missed-tackle rate. But when the rush doesn't get home, the coverage gets beat deep and over the middle: tight ends are averaging 0.72 EPA a target against it (31st) and second receivers 0.74 (32nd). Offenses know it and pass on Detroit more than almost anyone (pass rate over norm 3rd). This has happened before. The 2022 team paired a 6th-ranked offense with a 31st-ranked defense and won 9 games. The 2024 team that won 15 had a top-10 defense behind the same kind of offense.

The record says 5-2, but the underlying profile says roughly a .500 team. Net EPA is 19th at -0.002, the Lions are covering only 20% of the time (30th), and three of the five wins came by a field goal or a single point. The point differential (+23) implies about 4.8 wins, so this isn't pure luck. Still, the margin leans on special teams and a positive turnover differential that a defense with just 6 takeaways (24th) isn't generating on its own merits.

The last two weeks showed a different script. Beating Green Bay 20-17 and Minnesota 19-15 were grinders. In the Vikings game the passing game went negative (-4.2 EPA) and Detroit leaned on 230 rushing yards. The defense looked better in those two, but Minnesota's offense ranks 29th. The bigger story heading into November is the injury report. Jack Campbell (97% of snaps) is doubtful after a hospital stay for a neck injury, D.J. Reed (94%) is questionable with a hip, and both safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are on the report. A pass defense that was already broken may get thinner before it gets better.

strengths.title: Top-three passing offense with clean pockets
strengths.body: Goff is producing elite efficiency because he is rarely bothered. The line ranks 4th in pressure rate allowed, and the target tree is spread so defenses can't take away one option. This has been the franchise's identity since 2022 and is the most bankable trait on the roster.

strengths.title: A real pass rush and sure tackling
strengths.body: The front gets home at a top-10 clip and finishes, and the back end almost never whiffs in space. That keeps the floor from collapsing on what would otherwise be a historically bad defense, and it's the defense's path to stealing possessions. Losing Campbell and Wonnum would test how much of this survives.

strengths.title: Special teams tilting the field
strengths.body: The units rank 2nd in EPA a game. That is a hidden reason the point differential is positive despite a negative net EPA. Special teams value is noisier than offensive efficiency week to week, so don't count on it at this rate all year.

concerns.title: Coverage leaks explosives and middle targets
concerns.body: This is a genuine flaw, not a cost of the aggressive pass rush. The defense is 30th in explosive pass rate and bleeds to tight ends and secondary receivers, so offenses simply throw more against it. With Reed questionable and both starting safeties on the injury report, it is more likely to get worse than better in the short term.

concerns.title: Can't get off the field or hold in the red zone
concerns.body: Opponents convert nearly half their third downs and score touchdowns on most red-zone trips. That is why points allowed sit in the bottom seven even with the sack totals. It forces the offense to win shootouts, which it can do against average teams but not reliably against good ones.

concerns.title: Run game stalls in short yardage
concerns.body: The ground game succeeds often on standard downs (run success 3rd), but it gets stuffed at a bottom-three rate and fails on short yardage. That kills drives exactly where an elite offense should finish them, and a questionable center (Mays) won't help.

trend.note: The season opened with shootouts in which the offense carried a defense giving up 300-400 passing yards. The last two weeks flipped to grinding, low-scoring division wins, with the passing game sputtering against Minnesota's top-ranked defense. Which version shows up depends heavily on opponent quality.

nextGame.headline: Goff's clean pockets against the league's worst pass defense
nextGame.body:
Miami is 1-6 with a -0.175 net EPA (30th). The matchup lines up almost perfectly with Detroit's strength. The Dolphins rank dead last in pass EPA allowed and success rate allowed, have just 6 sacks (32nd), and get torched by tight ends (0.89 EPA a target, 32nd) and slot receivers. Malik Willis has started every game for an offense ranked 26th in EPA that runs far more than expected (pass rate over expected 31st). Its line ranks 30th in pressure allowed, and that is the opening for Detroit's pass rush. The Book has Detroit -7 with a 50.5 total, and the Lions have covered only 20% of the time this year.

Availability is the swing for the Lions' defense. Jack Campbell is doubtful after his neck injury, D.J. Reed is questionable, Branch and Wonnum are in concussion protocol as questionable, and Kerby Joseph was ruled out of the Vikings game. Center Cade Mays is questionable with a low ankle sprain. On Miami's side, starting tackle Kadyn Proctor (100% of snaps) is out with a concussion, which weakens an already leaky pass protection.

waysToWin.title: Throw at will against a toothless rush
waysToWin.body: Miami can't pressure the quarterback and ranks last in pass defense efficiency. Goff should have time to work the middle with LaPorta and St. Brown. Expect a game the Lions control through the air early, building a lead that forces Miami out of its run-first plan.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush feasts on a short-handed line
waysToWin.body: Miami allows pressure at a bottom-three rate and is now without its starting tackle. Detroit's top-10 rush can turn Willis' long-developing dropbacks into sacks and stalled drives, protecting a thin secondary from having to cover long.

waysToWin.title: Gibbs as a receiver and runner
waysToWin.body: Miami's defense gives lead backs more than their usual production and sees an outsized share of targets go to running backs. Gibbs out of the backfield is a clean way to stay on schedule and avoid the short-yardage stuffs.

waysToLose.title: Miami runs it and shortens the game
waysToLose.body: The Dolphins lean on the run and their backs get good yardage before contact. If Detroit's defense is without Campbell and Wonnum, Miami can sustain drives on Detroit's poor third-down defense, keep Goff on the sideline and turn it into a one-score fourth quarter.

waysToLose.title: Depleted secondary gives up explosives
waysToLose.body: Even a weak passing offense can hit big plays against a defense that ranks 30th in explosive pass rate. With Reed and the safeties hobbled, a couple of busted coverages could flip a game the Lions otherwise dominate.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone stalls and a sloppy road day
waysToLose.body: Detroit's short-yardage run game ranks 30th. The last two games featured giveaways and a negative passing day. If drives die inside the 20 and the Lions are trading field goals for touchdowns, a 1-6 team hangs around.

nextGame.watch: Whether Jack Campbell and D.J. Reed play. Without them, Miami's run game and an exposed secondary are the only realistic path to an upset.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is sustainable. Pass efficiency, pass protection and a deep target tree have been Detroit's constant across several seasons. The defense's coverage problems look equally real, and the injury list suggests it gets worse before Pacheco or anyone else returns in late December. The margin built on special teams and turnovers should shrink. The 5-2 start probably overstates a team whose net efficiency is mid-pack.

The schedule splits the rest of the season in two. Miami, Tennessee, Atlanta and a struggling Tampa offense are winnable. Four division games remain, three on the road, against Chicago (6-2), Minnesota (6-1) and Green Bay (5-3), plus New England. This looks like a 10-win team fighting for a wild card more than a division favorite, and how many of those late division games it wins will decide it.
swingFactors: Health of Campbell, Reed and the safeties
Results in four remaining division games
Whether special teams and turnover luck hold

confidence.note: Seven games, a consistent offense, but defensive injuries could reshape the second half.
